papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: A neural network model of hippocampal contributions to category learning
papers.research_question: What computational properties of the hippocampus might allow it to contribute to category learning, and how do the trisynaptic and monosynaptic pathways within the hippocampus support this learning?
papers.core_contribution: The trisynaptic pathway in the hippocampus is critical for remembering exemplar-specific information, while the monosynaptic pathway specializes in detecting category regularities, together supporting novel category learning.
papers.conclusion: The hippocampus supports category learning through complementary contributions of its pathways, with the TSP for arbitrary binding and the MSP for regularity detection.
papers.key_findings:
The trisynaptic pathway (TSP) is responsible for remembering unique features of individual exemplars.
The monosynaptic pathway (MSP) excels at categorization and generalization to novel exemplars.
The intact network (both pathways) shows a trade-off between categorization and recognition.
Representational similarity analysis shows that DG and CA3 represent items more distinctly, while CA1 shows more overlapping representations for items from the same category.
The model's performance across three different category learning paradigms mirrors human learning trajectories.
papers.limitation:
Simulations involved tasks with discrete-valued dimensions; future work should extend to continuous-valued dimensions.
The model does not include top-down modulation from prefrontal cortex.
future_direction: Extend to implementations of category learning tasks with continuous-valued dimensions.
Incorporate top-down modulation from prefrontal cortex.
Test the model in more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: In addition to its critical role in encoding individual episodes, the hippocampus is capable of extracting regularities across experiences. This ability is central to category learning, and a growing literature indicates that the hippocampus indeed makes important contributions to this form of learning. Using a neural network model that mirrors the anatomy of the hippocampus, we investigated the mechanisms by which the hippocampus may support novel category learning. We simulated three category learning paradigms and evaluated the network's ability to categorize and recognize specific exemplars in each. We found that the trisynaptic pathway within the hippocampus-connecting entorhinal cortex to dentate gyrus, CA3, and CA1-was critical for remembering exemplar-specific information, reflecting the rapid binding and pattern separation capabilities of this circuit. The monosynaptic pathway from entorhinal cortex to CA1, in contrast, specialized in detecting the regularities that define category structure across exemplars, supported by the use of distributed representations and a relatively slower learning rate. Together, the simulations provide an account of how the hippocampus and its constituent pathways support novel category learning.

papers.title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms behind hallucinations in language models, specifically regarding entity recognition and knowledge awareness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers entity recognition directions in the representation space that encode knowledge awareness and shows they causally affect knowledge refusal and hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models have internal representations of knowledge awareness that affect refusal and hallucinations, and that chat fine-tuning repurposes this existing mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders uncover directions in the representation space that detect whether the model recognizes an entity as known or unknown.
These entity recognition directions generalize across diverse entity types (players, movies, cities, songs).
The directions causally affect knowledge refusal: steering can induce the model to refuse on known entities or hallucinate on unknown entities.
The directions disrupt the attention of downstream heads in the factual recall circuit, suppressing attribute extraction.
Early entity recognition directions regulate the model's expression of knowledge uncertainty, and uncertainty directions are predictive of incorrect answers.
papers.limitation: The methodology for labeling entities as known or unknown might introduce inaccuracies, as the model could guess attributes or fail to recall specific attributes while knowing about the entity.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.

papers.title: Semantic Systematicity in Connectionist Language Production
papers.research_question: Can a connectionist model achieve systematicity (semantic and syntactic generalization) in language production?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a connectionist sentence production model that uses rich situation model representations, demonstrating semantic and syntactic systematicity (generalization) in language production.
papers.conclusion: Connectionist models can achieve systematicity in language production when provided with structured semantic representations that capture regularities of the world.
papers.key_findings:
The model can produce novel sentences for previously unseen situations, including in a different voice (active vs. passive).
The model can produce words in syntactic roles with which they were not seen during training.
The model fails to produce sentences describing impossible situations, instead producing similar plausible sentences.
The model's systematic behavior is attributed to the regularities in the semantic representations derived from a structured microworld.
The model can typically produce all sentence encodings related to a novel message representation, not just a single sentence.
papers.limitation: The model completely fails to produce sentences describing impossible situations, instead producing similar sentences describing plausible scenarios.
papers.abstract: Decades of studies trying to define the extent to which artificial neural networks can exhibit systematicity suggest that systematicity can be achieved by connectionist models but not by default. Here we present a novel connectionist model of sentence production that employs rich situation model representations originally proposed for modeling systematicity in comprehension. The high performance of our model demonstrates that such representations are also well suited to model language production. Furthermore, the model can produce multiple novel sentences for previously unseen situations, including in a different voice (actives vs. passive) and with words in new syntactic roles, thus demonstrating semantic and syntactic generalization and arguably systematicity. Our results provide yet further evidence that such connectionist approaches can achieve systematicity, in production as well as comprehension. We propose our positive results to be a consequence of the regularities of the microworld from which the semantic representations are derived, which provides a sufficient structure from which the neural network can interpret novel inputs.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus. This nascent thesis proposes that facts are recalled from the training corpus through the MLP weights in a manner resembling key-value memory, implying in effect that "knowledge" is stored in the network. Furthermore, by modifying the MLP modules, one can control the language model's generation of factual information. The plausibility of the KN thesis has been demonstrated by the success of KN-inspired model editing methods (Dai et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). We find that this thesis is, at best, an oversimplification. Not only have we found that we can edit the expression of certain linguistic phenomena using the same model editing methods but, through a more comprehensive evaluation, we have found that the KN thesis does not adequately explain the process of factual expression. While it is possible to argue that the MLP weights store complex patterns that are interpretable both syntactically and semantically, these patterns do not constitute "knowledge." To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge representation process, we must look beyond the MLP weights and explore recent models' complex layer structures and attention mechanisms.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Number Representations in LLMs: A Computational Parallel to Human Perception
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) encode numerical values in a logarithmic-like structure, similar to the human mental number line hypothesis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode numerical values with structured, sublinear compression akin to the human logarithmic mental number line, a pattern detectable via unsupervised methods like PCA but often obscured by supervised linear probes like PLS.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode numerical values with structured compression similar to the human mental number line, but this sublinearity is only detectable through unsupervised dimensionality reduction methods like PCA that preserve geometric relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Numerical embeddings in LLMs exhibit higher explained variance and stronger monotonicity compared to random letter sequences, indicating a structured number line.
The Scaling Rate Index (β) reveals sublinear scaling (β < 1) in many models, showing compression where distances between numbers decrease as values increase.
PCA captures the underlying sublinear structure of numerical representations, while PLS, as a supervised linear probe, often misses this non-uniformity by optimizing for covariance with the target.
Layer-wise analysis shows that the sublinear encoding is consistent across layers, with the layer of highest explained variance also showing strong monotonicity.
In real-world tasks, birth year data shows systematic sublinear encoding, while population data is less structured due to context-dependence and approximate expressions.
papers.abstract: Humans are believed to perceive numbers on a logarithmic mental number line, where smaller values are represented with greater resolution than larger ones. This cognitive bias, supported by neuroscience and behavioral studies, suggests that numerical magnitudes are processed in a sublinear fashion rather than on a uniform linear scale. Inspired by this hypothesis, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit a similar logarithmic-like structure in their internal numerical representations. By analyzing how numerical values are encoded across different layers of LLMs, we apply dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and PLS followed by geometric regression to uncover latent structures in the learned embeddings. Our findings reveal that the model's numerical representations exhibit sublinear spacing, with distances between values aligning with a logarithmic scale. This suggests that LLMs, much like humans, may encode numbers in a compressed, non-uniform manner.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: The Shape of Beliefs: Geometry, Dynamics, and Interventions along Representation Manifolds of Language Models' Posteriors
papers.research_question: How are prompt-conditioned beliefs encoded in representation space, how do they update with new evidence, and how can interventions reshape them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that beliefs in LLMs are encoded as curved manifolds in representation space, and that linear steering often fails to preserve the intended belief family, while geometry-aware steering based on linear field probes is more effective.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction, highlighting the importance of geometry-aware methods for interpretability and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Belief manifolds for distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) are curved in representation space.
Linear field probes can tile the manifold and decode parameters with high accuracy and smooth variation.
When the input distribution changes, the model updates its beliefs along trajectories on the manifold, with different timescales for mean and variance.
Linear steering can push activations off-manifold, causing coupled shifts in other parameters (e.g., variance).
Geometry-aware steering using linear field probes better preserves the intended belief family and avoids unintended coupled shifts.
papers.limitation:
Relies on small open-source base models and focuses on a restricted family of prompt distributions (time-series), which may not capture the diversity of internal geometries in other settings.
The assumption that beliefs live on manifolds indexable by interpretable parameters may not hold in natural language tasks where latent variables are not fully parameterizable.
Does not investigate causal attribution to uncover which neuronal structure or circuits are responsible for the observed geometry.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) represent prompt-conditioned beliefs (posteriors over answers and claims), but we lack a mechanistic account of how these beliefs are encoded in representation space, how they update with new evidence, and how interventions reshape them. We study a controlled setting in which Llama-3.2 generates samples from a normal distribution by implicitly inferring its parameters (mean and standard deviation) given only samples from the distribution in context. We find representations of curved "belief manifolds" for these parameters form with sufficient in-context learning and study how the model adapts when the distribution suddenly changes. While standard linear steering often pushes the model off-manifold and induces coupled, out-of-distribution shifts, geometry and field-aware steering better preserves the intended belief family. Our work demonstrates an example of linear field probing (LFP) as a simple approach to tile the data manifold and make interventions that respect the underlying geometry. We conclude that rich structure emerges naturally in LLMs and that purely linear concept representations are often an inadequate abstraction.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Information theoretic study of the neural geometry induced by category learning
papers.research_question: What are the optimal properties of neural representations induced by category learning from an information theoretic perspective?
papers.core_contribution: Minimizing the Bayesian cost in categorization leads to maximizing mutual information between categories and neural activity, causing neural space expansion near decision boundaries and explaining categorical perception.
papers.conclusion: Category learning optimizes neural representations by maximizing mutual information, leading to appropriate representation spaces and metrics, with expansion near decision boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
The Bayesian cost can be decomposed into coding and decoding components.
Mutual information between categories and neural code can be expressed as a sum of terms for representation space and metrics.
Category learning induces expansion of neural space near decision boundaries, enhancing discrimination.
Numerical experiments show that Fisher information of the neural population aligns with category boundaries.
The approach relates to the information bottleneck method in the limit of infinite beta.
papers.limitation:
Results are based on exact probability distributions and should be reconsidered with finite examples.
Effect of noise at any stage of processing and noise correlations need to be studied.
Estimating the categorical Fisher information Fcat is challenging.
Understanding the effect of noise correlations on neural geometry is an open issue.
future_direction: Reconsider results in the context of learning with a finite set of examples.
Study the effect of noise at any stage of processing, including noise correlations.
Find ways of estimating the categorical Fisher information Fcat.
Understand the effect of noise correlations on the geometry of neural space.
papers.abstract: Categorization is an important topic both for biological and artificial neural networks. Here, we take an information theoretic approach to assess the efficiency of the representations induced by category learning. We show that one can decompose the relevant Bayesian cost into two components, one for the coding part and one for the decoding part. Minimizing the coding cost implies maximizing the mutual information between the set of categories and the neural activities. We analytically show that this mutual information can be written as the sum of two terms that can be interpreted as (i) finding an appropriate representation space, and, (ii) building a representation with the appropriate metrics, based on the neural Fisher information on this space. One main consequence is that category learning induces an expansion of neural space near decision boundaries. Finally, we provide numerical illustrations that show how Fisher information of the coding neural population aligns with the boundaries between categories.

papers.title: Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve factual knowledge? The paper investigates the mechanistic story behind factual recall, focusing on prompts of the form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of ____.'
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall in LLMs is achieved through an additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs), termed the 'additive motif', and extends direct logit attribution to attribute attention head outputs to individual source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall in LLMs is achieved through additive combination of multiple independent mechanisms, and this additive motif may be a general principle in how models compute.
papers.key_findings:
There are four distinct mechanisms (subject heads, relation heads, mixed heads, MLPs) that additively combine to produce factual recall.
Each mechanism independently contributes to the correct logit, and their sum results in constructive interference, even if individual mechanisms are insufficient alone.
The additive motif explains why models often produce incorrect attributes alongside correct ones.
Extending direct logit attribution to attribute head outputs to source tokens reveals mixed heads as two separate additive updates from subject and relation tokens.
The work highlights a limitation of narrow circuit analysis that ignores multiple sources of information in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small and hand-written, which may limit generalizability.
The analysis is limited to a specific prompting format and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Understanding correlation and superposition in feature representations
Understanding MLP neurons in detail
Studying how different prompting setups affect factual recall mechanisms
papers.abstract: How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form `Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interfere on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call `mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens.

papers.title: Semantic Structure in Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: Do semantic features in LLM embeddings exhibit a low-dimensional structure similar to human semantic ratings, and does the geometric alignment of features predict off-target effects when steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantic features in LLM embeddings are low-dimensional and entangled similarly to human semantic ratings, and that off-target effects from steering are predictable based on cosine similarity between feature vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic associations in LLM embeddings are relatively low-dimensional, and accounting for the geometric structure of features is essential for anticipating and mitigating unintended consequences of feature steering.
papers.key_findings:
Projections of words on semantic directions defined by antonym pairs correlate highly with human ratings.
These projections reduce to a 3-dimensional subspace within LLM embeddings, closely resembling patterns from human survey responses.
Shifting tokens along one semantic direction causes off-target effects on geometrically aligned features proportional to their cosine similarity.
Whitening embeddings reduces correlation with human ratings, suggesting non-orthogonality reflects semantic structure rather than noise.
The correlation structure between features in LLM embeddings is similar to that in human ratings.
papers.limitation: The study only analyzes embedding spaces and does not consider how feature geometries are transformed across model layers or dynamically reconfigured by context.
future_direction: Study how feature geometries transform across model layers and components.
Investigate how the relations between features in activation space are dynamically reconfigured by the preceding tokens in the context sequence.
Assemble features into conceptual maps to advance understanding of how LLMs make sense of the world.
papers.abstract: Psychological research consistently finds that human ratings of words across diverse semantic scales can be reduced to a low-dimensional form with relatively little information loss. We find that the semantic associations encoded in the embedding matrices of large language models (LLMs) exhibit a similar structure. We show that the projections of words on semantic directions defined by antonym pairs (e.g. kind - cruel) correlate highly with human ratings, and further find that these projections effectively reduce to a 3-dimensional subspace within LLM embeddings, closely resembling the patterns derived from human survey responses. Moreover, we find that shifting tokens along one semantic direction causes off-target effects on geometrically aligned features proportional to their cosine similarity. These findings suggest that semantic features are entangled within LLMs similarly to how they are interconnected in human language, and a great deal of semantic information, despite its apparent complexity, is surprisingly low-dimensional. Furthermore, accounting for this semantic structure may prove essential for avoiding unintended consequences when steering features.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration.
