VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
papers.research_question: Why do geometric structures (circles, loops, manifolds) arise in the internal representations of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that translation symmetry in pairwise co-occurrence statistics of natural language explains the emergence of geometric structures (e.g., circles, manifolds) in the internal representations of language models.
papers.conclusion: Representational manifolds have a universal origin: symmetry in the statistics of natural data.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical observation of representation manifolds (circles, loops) and linear coordinate decoding in shallow word embedding models like word2vec.
Evidence that words embodying a continuous latent concept have pairwise co-occurrence statistics that exhibit translation symmetry.
Analytical expressions that predict the representational geometry directly from these translation symmetric statistics.
Validation that the predicted representational structure is present and stable in both word embedding models and deep transformer-based models.
Theoretical and empirical demonstration that representation manifolds are robust to significant perturbations in co-occurrence statistics, explained by collective effects involving many words.
papers.abstract: Although learned representations underlie neural networks' success, their fundamental properties remain poorly understood. A striking example is the emergence of simple geometric structures in LLM representations: for example, calendar months organize into a circle, years form a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and cities' latitudes and longitudes can be decoded by a linear probe. We show that the statistics of language exhibit a translation symmetry -- e.g., the co-occurrence probability of two months depends only on the time interval between them -- and we prove that the latter governs the aforementioned geometric structures in high-dimensional word embedding models. Moreover, we find that these structures persist even when the co-occurrence statistics are strongly perturbed (for example, by removing all sentences in which two months appear together) and at moderate embedding dimension. We show that this robustness naturally emerges if the co-occurrence statistics are collectively controlled by an underlying continuous latent variable. We empirically validate this theoretical framework in word embedding models, text embedding models, and large language models.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the connection between pretraining data frequency and the formation of linear representations of factual relations in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The formation of linear representations for factual recall in language models is strongly correlated with pretraining term frequencies, and measuring these representations allows prediction of term frequencies in the pretraining corpus.
papers.conclusion: Linear representations of factual triplets in LMs are connected to pretraining frequencies, which can guide interpretability work and enable prediction of term frequencies in closed-data models.
papers.key_findings:
The development of linear representations for factual recall relations in LMs is related to frequency as well as model size.
Linear representations form at predictable frequency thresholds during training, regardless of when this threshold is met, and correlate strongly with recall accuracy.
Measuring the extent to which a relation is represented linearly allows prediction of the approximate frequencies of individual terms in the pretraining corpus, even without access to the training data.
The predictive signal from linear representations is stronger than that from log probabilities and task accuracies alone.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on factual relations and leaves non-factual relations (e.g., gender stereotypes) for future work.
The regression model provides approximate frequency predictions within bounds, not exact counts.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to non-factual relations.
Improve the bounds of predicted frequencies.
Understand if and when LMs use non-linear methods to solve tasks.
papers.abstract: Pretraining data has a direct impact on the behaviors and quality of language models (LMs), but we only understand the most basic principles of this relationship. While most work focuses on pretraining data's effect on downstream task behavior, we investigate its relationship to LM representations. Previous work has discovered that, in language models, some concepts are encoded `linearly' in the representations, but what factors cause these representations to form? We study the connection between pretraining data frequency and models' linear representations of factual relations. We find evidence that the formation of linear representations is strongly connected to pretraining term frequencies; specifically for subject-relation-object fact triplets, both subject-object co-occurrence frequency and in-context learning accuracy for the relation are highly correlated with linear representations. This is the case across all phases of pretraining. In OLMo-7B and GPT-J, we discover that a linear representation consistently (but not exclusively) forms when the subjects and objects within a relation co-occur at least 1k and 2k times, respectively, regardless of when these occurrences happen during pretraining. Finally, we train a regression model on measurements of linear representation quality in fully-trained LMs that can predict how often a term was seen in pretraining. Our model achieves low error even on inputs from a different model with a different pretraining dataset, providing a new method for estimating properties of the otherwise-unknown training data of closed-data models. We conclude that the strength of linear representations in LMs contains signal about the models' pretraining corpora that may provide new avenues for controlling and improving model behavior: particularly, manipulating the models' training data to meet specific frequency thresholds.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Human-like object concept representations emerge naturally in multimodal large language models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like object concept representations through exposure to vast amounts of linguistic and multimodal data.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like object concept representations, as evidenced by low-dimensional embeddings derived from similarity judgments that are interpretable, show semantic clustering, and align with human neural activity patterns.
papers.conclusion: LLMs and MLLMs develop human-like conceptual representations of natural objects, with multimodal learning leading to more nuanced and brain-aligned representations.
papers.key_findings:
The derived 66-dimensional embeddings from LLM and MLLM similarity judgments are stable and predictive of both single-trial behavior and object similarity scores.
The embeddings exhibit spontaneous semantic clustering, mirroring human mental representations of object categories.
The dimensions underlying the embeddings are interpretable, reflecting semantic, perceptual, and spatial properties of objects.
There is a strong correspondence between the core dimensions identified in LLMs/MLLMs and those from human similarity judgments.
The model embeddings show strong alignment with neural activity patterns in functionally defined, category-selective brain regions (e.g., EBA, PPA, RSC, FFA).
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> The conceptualization and categorization of natural objects in the human mind have long intrigued cognitive scientists and neuroscientists, offering crucial insights into human perception and cognition. Recently, the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has raised the attractive question of whether these models can also develop human-like object representations through exposure to vast amounts of linguistic and multimodal data. In this study, we combined behavioral and neuroimaging analysis methods to uncover how the object concept representations in LLMs correlate with those of humans. By collecting large-scale datasets of 4.7 million triplet judgments from LLM and Multimodal LLM (MLLM), we were able to derive low-dimensional embeddings that capture the underlying similarity structure of 1,854 natural objects. The resulting 66-dimensional embeddings were found to be highly stable and predictive, and exhibited semantic clustering akin to human mental representations. Interestingly, the interpretability of the dimensions underlying these embeddings suggests that LLM and MLLM have developed human-like conceptual representations of natural objects. Further analysis demonstrated strong alignment between the identified model embeddings and neural activity patterns in many functionally defined brain ROIs (e.g., EBA, PPA, RSC and FFA). This provides compelling evidence that the object representations in LLMs, while not identical to those in the human, share fundamental commonalities that reflect key schemas of human conceptual knowledge. This study advances our understanding of machine intelligence and informs the development of more human-like artificial cognitive systems.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Neurons Speak in Ranges: Breaking Free from Discrete Neuronal Attribution
papers.research_question: How does polysemanticity in neurons affect discrete neuron-concept attribution, and can activation ranges enable more precise interpretation and manipulation in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuronLens, a range-based framework for neuron interpretation and manipulation, showing that concept-specific activation ranges allow precise attribution and intervention with reduced collateral damage compared to neuron-level masking.
papers.conclusion: Range-based attribution enables more precise interpretability and targeted manipulation in LLMs, overcoming limitations of discrete neuron-to-concept mapping.
papers.key_findings:
Neuronal activations in LLMs form concept-conditioned, Gaussian-like distributions with minimal overlap across concepts.
Polysemantic neurons exhibit distinct activation ranges for different concepts, enabling fine-grained attribution.
Range-based interventions (e.g., activation range masking) effectively suppress target concepts while causing substantially less degradation to auxiliary concepts and overall model performance than full neuron masking.
The method reduces unintended interference on auxiliary concepts by up to 25 percentage points compared to neuron masking in some settings.
Range-based interventions preserve general capabilities, maintaining or improving performance on benchmarks like MMLU with minor increases in perplexity.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for improving their trustworthiness and utility. Prior work has primarily focused on mapping individual neurons to discrete semantic concepts. However, such mappings struggle to handle the inherent polysemanticity in LLMs, where individual neurons encode multiple, distinct concepts. Through a comprehensive analysis of both encoder and decoder-based LLMs across diverse datasets, we observe that even highly salient neurons, identified via various attribution techniques for specific semantic concepts, consistently exhibit polysemantic behavior. Importantly, activation magnitudes for fine-grained concepts follow distinct, often Gaussian-like distributions with minimal overlap. This observation motivates a shift from neuron attribution to range-based interpretation. We hypothesize that interpreting and manipulating neuron activation ranges would enable more precise interpretability and targeted interventions in LLMs. To validate our hypothesis, we introduce NeuronLens, a novel range-based interpretation and manipulation framework that provides a finer view of neuron activation distributions to localize concept attribution within a neuron. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that NeuronLens significantly reduces unintended interference, while maintaining precise manipulation of targeted concepts, outperforming neuron attribution.

papers.title: Learning to Trust Your Feelings: Leveraging Self-awareness in LLMs for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How well can LLMs discern and express their internal knowledge state to mitigate factual hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLMs can discern their internal knowledge state with high accuracy but often fail to express it, leading to hallucinations. It introduces the RLKF training framework, which uses knowledge feedback via reinforcement learning to improve model factuality and honesty.
papers.conclusion: RLKF is effective in improving the model's utilization of its internal knowledge state, enhancing performance in knowledge and honesty related tasks, and is a promising solution for hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are highly adept at discerning their internal knowledge, with over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing.
DreamCatcher, an automatic hallucination detection tool, achieves 81% agreement with human annotators.
RLKF training enhances the factuality and honesty of LLMs, improving performance on knowledge-based tasks.
RLKF avoids the 'alignment tax' and improves benchmark performance on various tasks.
The reward model can quickly achieve high accuracy by utilizing internal knowledge state.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to discern and express their internal knowledge state, a key factor in countering factual hallucination and ensuring reliable application of LLMs. We observe a robust self-awareness of internal knowledge state in LLMs, evidenced by over 85% accuracy in knowledge probing. However, LLMs often fail to express their internal knowledge during generation, leading to factual hallucinations. We develop an automated hallucination annotation tool, Dreamcatcher, which merges knowledge probing and consistency checking methods to rank factual preference data. Using knowledge preference as reward, We propose a Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback (RLKF) training framework, leveraging reinforcement learning to enhance the factuality and honesty of LLMs. Our experiments across multiple models show that RLKF training effectively enhances the ability of models to utilize their internal knowledge state, boosting performance in a variety of knowledge-based and honesty-related tasks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
papers.research_question: Do LLMs exhibit differences in internal activations when processing prompts associated with different Bloom levels? At what depth do representations of cognitive complexity emerge? Is Bloom-level information linearly recoverable from hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probing shows that cognitive complexity levels (Bloom's Taxonomy) are linearly separable in the residual stream activations of LLMs, emerging early in the forward pass and becoming more separable across layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a measurable, linearly separable internal representation of cognitive complexity that aligns closely with Bloom’s Taxonomy, validating it as a framework for auditing the internal mechanics of artificial cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Linear classifiers achieve ~95% mean accuracy in classifying Bloom levels from residual stream activations.
Cognitive complexity emerges early in the forward pass (around layer 5) and remains stable in deeper layers.
Misclassifications occur predominantly between adjacent Bloom levels, indicating that the representations preserve the ordinal structure of cognitive complexity.
Geometric analysis shows increasing centroid distances between adjacent Bloom levels across layers, indicating progressive disentanglement.
The findings are consistent across four different LLM architectures.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on decoder-only transformer architectures and English educational questions.
Generalizability to other architectures (e.g., encoder-only or encoder-decoder) and languages remains to be established.
Linear probes demonstrate linear accessibility but do not prove that the model uses this information causally during generation.
Methodology examines only the residual stream, leaving attention patterns and MLP internals as areas for future investigation.
future_direction: Causal intervention studies to validate whether the cognitive representations are functionally utilized by the model.
Cross-lingual and cross-domain analysis to establish universality of the findings.
Investigating attention patterns and MLP internals.
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of cognitive complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different cognitive levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve approximately 95% mean accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing strong evidence that cognitive level is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model resolves the cognitive difficulty of a prompt early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

papers.title: Analogical Reasoning Inside Large Language Models: Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction
papers.research_question: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor internal, invariant representations of abstract concepts like those used in analogical reasoning, and how can such representations be extracted and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Concept Vectors (CVs), distilled from early-to-mid attention heads using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), which provide invariant linear representations for verbal concepts (e.g., antonym) and can causally guide model behavior. It finds that abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' lack such invariant representations, limiting generalization.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs form invariant linear representations (CVs) for verbal concepts, they lack such representations for more abstract relational concepts like 'previous' and 'next', which hinders their ability to generalize analogical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Function Vectors (FVs) are not invariant to low-level input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice format) and encode multiple task attributes beyond the latent concept.
Activation patching, used to identify FVs, localizes components causally important for output but fails to identify heads encoding latent conceptual information.
Concept Vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts are invariant to low-level transformations and emerge in early-to-mid layers, acting as feature detectors that can represent the correct concept even when the model's final output is incorrect.
CVs can causally guide model behavior in-context and are more portable across low-level task variations than FVs, though FVs are more effective in zero-shot settings.
Abstract concepts like 'previous' and 'next' do not form invariant linear representations in the models studied, which correlates with poor generalization on tasks requiring abstraction, such as letter-string analogies.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses exclusively on linear representations, despite evidence that LLM representations can be nonlinear, potentially missing nonlinear encodings of abstract concepts.
Conclusions are restricted to the Llama-3.1 8B and 70B models, leaving generalizability to other architectures untested.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning relies on conceptual abstractions, but it is unclear whether Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor such internal representations. We explore distilled representations from LLM activations and find that function vectors (FVs; Todd et al., 2024) - compact representations for in-context learning (ICL) tasks - are not invariant to simple input changes (e.g., open-ended vs. multiple-choice), suggesting they capture more than pure concepts. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA), we localize a small set of attention heads that encode invariant concept vectors (CVs) for verbal concepts like "antonym". These CVs function as feature detectors that operate independently of the final output - meaning that a model may form a correct internal representation yet still produce an incorrect output. Furthermore, CVs can be used to causally guide model behaviour. However, for more abstract concepts like "previous" and "next", we do not observe invariant linear representations, a finding we link to generalizability issues LLMs display within these domains.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mathematical theory of semantic development in deep linear networks, showing how hierarchical differentiation and other semantic phenomena emerge from the interaction of statistical structure and nonlinear learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, providing analytic insight into how statistical structure interacts with nonlinear deep learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Deep linear networks exhibit hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions.
The model accounts for semantic illusions during periods of developmental stasis.
Item typicality and category coherence emerge as factors controlling semantic processing speed.
Patterns of inductive projection change over development.
The similarity structure of internal representations is conserved across networks trained optimally.
papers.limitation: The linear model cannot capture complex nonlinear semantic phenomena such as context dependence, theory of mind, causal reasoning, and event structure binding.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of more complex neural circuits to explain higher-level cognitive computations.
papers.abstract: An extensive body of empirical research has revealed remarkable regularities in the acquisition, organization, deployment, and neural representation of human semantic knowledge, thereby raising a fundamental conceptual question: What are the theoretical principles governing the ability of neural networks to acquire, organize, and deploy abstract knowledge by integrating across many individual experiences? We address this question by mathematically analyzing the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear networks. We find exact solutions to this learning dynamics that yield a conceptual explanation for the prevalence of many disparate phenomena in semantic cognition, including the hierarchical differentiation of concepts through rapid developmental transitions, the ubiquity of semantic illusions between such transitions, the emergence of item typicality and category coherence as factors controlling the speed of semantic processing, changing patterns of inductive projection over development, and the conservation of semantic similarity in neural representations across species. Thus, surprisingly, our simple neural model qualitatively recapitulates many diverse regularities underlying semantic development, while providing analytic insight into how the statistical structure of an environment can interact with nonlinear deep-learning dynamics to give rise to these regularities.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: How Large Language Models Encode Context Knowledge? A Layer-Wise Probing Study
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode context knowledge across different layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a layer-wise probing framework to study how LLMs encode context knowledge, finding that more context knowledge is encoded in upper layers and that knowledge-related entity tokens encode knowledge earlier, with knowledge spreading to other tokens via attention.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel layer-wise probing framework for explaining how LLMs encode context knowledge, demonstrating that LLMs encode more knowledge in upper layers and transfer knowledge from entity tokens to other tokens, with retention diminishing with irrelevant evidence.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers.
LLMs primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers.
LLMs gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence.
Base models have lower capability to encode knowledge through prompting compared to chat models.
The long-term memory capability of LLMs degrades when irrelevant evidence is introduced.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical mechanism behind the observed phenomena remains an open issue.
Experiments are limited to LLaMA 2 models, ignoring other SOTA models.
future_direction: Mathematical understanding of the role of self-attention in knowledge transfer.
Experiments on more PLMs (e.g., PaLM, OPT, Pythia).
papers.abstract: Previous work has showcased the intriguing capability of large language models (LLMs) in retrieving facts and processing context knowledge. However, only limited research exists on the layer-wise capability of LLMs to encode knowledge, which challenges our understanding of their internal mechanisms. In this paper, we devote the first attempt to investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs through probing tasks. We leverage the powerful generative capability of ChatGPT to construct probing datasets, providing diverse and coherent evidence corresponding to various facts. We employ $\mathcal V$-usable information as the validation metric to better reflect the capability in encoding context knowledge across different layers. Our experiments on conflicting and newly acquired knowledge show that LLMs: (1) prefer to encode more context knowledge in the upper layers; (2) primarily encode context knowledge within knowledge-related entity tokens at lower layers while progressively expanding more knowledge within other tokens at upper layers; and (3) gradually forget the earlier context knowledge retained within the intermediate layers when provided with irrelevant evidence. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Jometeorie/probing_llama.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: What Are Large Language Models Mapping to in the Brain? A Case Against Over-Reliance on Brain Scores
papers.research_question: What are large language models mapping to in the brain? The paper questions whether high brain scores indicate shared computational principles between LLMs and human language processing or are explained by simpler, theoretically uninteresting features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that high brain scores of LLMs on neural datasets can be largely explained by simple features like sentence length, position, and static word embeddings, cautioning against over-interpreting these scores as evidence of shared computational principles with human language processing.
papers.conclusion: Brain scores on the analyzed datasets should be interpreted with caution, and analyses using brain scores should be accompanied by a systematic deconstruction of neural encoding performance against simple features to avoid over-interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled train-test splits are severely affected by temporal autocorrelation, and a trivial feature (OASM) that encodes this autocorrelation outperforms LLMs and accounts for most of their explained neural variance.
Untrained GPT2-XL's brain score is fully accounted for by two simple features: sentence length and sentence position.
Trained GPT2-XL's brain score is largely explained by sentence length, sentence position, and static word embeddings; only a small additional amount is explained by sense embeddings and contextual syntactic representations.
On the Fedorenko dataset, word position explains all of the untrained and most of the trained GPT2-XL neural predictivity.
On the Blank dataset, GPT2-XL predicts neural activity at chance levels when using contiguous train-test splits.
papers.limitation:
The method of examining how much neural variance an LLM predicts over simple features scales poorly when the number of feature spaces is large.
The procedure may be biased against regressions with many feature spaces due to noise in neural data and low sample sizes.
The study did not analyze datasets with large amounts of neural data per participant, where the gap between simple and complex features might be larger.
papers.abstract: Given the remarkable capabilities of large language models (LLMs), there has been a growing interest in evaluating their similarity to the human brain. One approach towards quantifying this similarity is by measuring how well a model predicts neural signals, also called "brain score". Internal representations from LLMs achieve state-of-the-art brain scores, leading to speculation that they share computational principles with human language processing. This inference is only valid if the subset of neural activity predicted by LLMs reflects core elements of language processing. Here, we question this assumption by analyzing three neural datasets used in an impactful study on LLM-to-brain mappings, with a particular focus on an fMRI dataset where participants read short passages. We first find that when using shuffled train-test splits, as done in previous studies with these datasets, a trivial feature that encodes temporal autocorrelation not only outperforms LLMs but also accounts for the majority of neural variance that LLMs explain. We therefore use contiguous splits moving forward. Second, we explain the surprisingly high brain scores of untrained LLMs by showing they do not account for additional neural variance beyond two simple features: sentence length and sentence position. This undermines evidence used to claim that the transformer architecture biases computations to be more brain-like. Third, we find that brain scores of trained LLMs on this dataset can largely be explained by sentence length, position, and pronoun-dereferenced static word embeddings; a small, additional amount is explained by sense-specific embeddings and contextual representations of sentence structure.
